extracted.intended_audience: general readers and people interested in net neutrality, FCC rulemaking, and media influence
extracted.subtask_description: A Wikipedia article summarizing John Oliver's 'Net Neutrality II' Last Week Tonight segment, its arguments about net neutrality and Title II reclassification, and the effects on the FCC notice-and-comment process (mass comments, spambots, investigations, and the eventual repeal).

rubrics_metrics.name: Net neutrality principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Under net neutrality laws, ISPs have to treat all web traffic the same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explained via Tay Zonday's example: an ISP cannot favor one search engine by slowing traffic to others. Oliver framed net neutrality as preventing ISPs and big companies from blocking or restricting users' online actions or preventing competition from small companies (example: Ancestry.com crushing a new site).

rubrics_metrics.name: Title II reclassification as regulatory basis
rubrics_metrics.description: Reclassifying broadband as a telecommunication service (Title II of the Communications Act of 1934) provides an enforceable legal footing to preserve net neutrality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes the FCC's 2015 reclassification that treated broadband as a utility and that Oliver presented reclassification as the only way to effectively regulate ISPs. Context includes Comcast v. FCC and discussion of Pai's move to reverse the classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical evidence of throttling or blocking
rubrics_metrics.description: Demonstrable instances of ISPs throttling or blocking services are relevant evidence in favor of regulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oliver refuted Ajit Pai's claim that there was no evidence of throttling by citing reporting (Bloomberg) about Verizon, AT&T, and T-Mobile blocking access to Google Wallet because it competed with their own service, showing concrete examples that support regulatory intervention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voluntary terms-of-service statements are insufficient protection
rubrics_metrics.description: A proposal that ISPs merely include voluntary statements in their terms of service promising not to throttle or block content is inadequate to secure net neutrality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oliver mocked this alternative as making net neutrality 'as binding as a proposal on The Bachelor,' arguing that voluntary promises lack enforceability compared to Title II reclassification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims about regulation reducing investment must be scrutinized
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements that net neutrality rules caused decreased broadband investment should be evaluated against evidence and industry statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article cites Ajit Pai's rationale that rules reduced investment and counters it with responses from Senator Brian Schatz and a Verizon CFO (Francis J. Shammo) whose comments indicated the rules did not affect Verizon's business, illustrating the need to check industry claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity and legitimacy of public comments
rubrics_metrics.description: The legitimacy of comments submitted during notice-and-comment matters; fake or automated (spambot) comments can distort the administrative record and may be subject to disregard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page documents over 1 million spambot comments and estimates of up to 7 million fake comments using templates and duplicate addresses. Because of widespread doubts about authenticity, the FCC considered disregarding comments and adversaries (e.g., New York AG) undertook investigations; verifying commenter identity and filtering duplicates is central to assessing the public record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effects of media-driven mass comment campaigns
rubrics_metrics.description: Large-scale comment surges inspired by media (e.g., John Oliver) can alter rulemaking dynamics—prompting extensions, public attention, and technological stress—but also attract inauthentic comments and scrutiny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oliver's segment reportedly produced hundreds of thousands to millions of extra comments, led to extension of the comment period (to August 30), and coincided with FCC site outages and debates over DDoS attacks vs. traffic surges; mass campaigns can therefore have both mobilizing and complicating effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency transparency and investigative remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should investigate and disclose data about outages, comment handling, and the integrity of the record; affected parties may use FOIA or state AG investigations to seek information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article references a BuzzFeed FOIA lawsuit after the FCC refused to publish data related to the outage and the New York Attorney General creating tools and conducting investigations into false comments, highlighting transparency and oversight as remedies when procedural irregularities occur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public comments do not guarantee policy outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Even very large public comment volumes in support of a rule do not ensure the agency will retain or adopt that rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Despite millions of comments supporting net neutrality and polls showing public support, the FCC announced plans and then voted to repeal the 2015 net neutrality rules in November and December 2017, illustrating limits of comment-driven influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tonality and content standards for effective advocacy
rubrics_metrics.description: The tone and content of submitted comments matter; racist, abusive, or prank submissions undermine credibility and are counterproductive to advocacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oliver admonished viewers that racist comments or offensive jokes (and fake names/addresses used in prank comments) do not help the cause. The article cites many examples of fake, offensive, or prank submissions and Oliver's call to refrain from adding more comments when appropriate.
